At Antino Labs, more than 1,000 payments a day run through backend services he built, connecting an internal platform to two outside payment companies that each had their own request format and error handling. He normalised those differences so everything downstream could treat them the same way.

At Antino Labs, payments were failing at random and some customers were charged twice. He reproduced the fault, traced it to endpoints that could not handle the same request arriving more than once, and rebuilt them to recognise and ignore repeats. Failed payments fell 30 percent. This is his clearest example of debugging a production issue end to end: symptom, reproduction, root cause, fix, measured result.

At Antino Labs he put 6 payment methods behind one interface, with new providers addable without rewriting what already worked, because each provider plugs in as a separate module. This is an example of designing for extension rather than rewriting.

Rivora is a collaborative recording platform, built end to end in Java and Spring Boot with REST services, MongoDB storage, Redis caching, and a React interface on top. Node.js worker microservices handle the media pipeline and Kafka carries work between the services. It runs on Kubernetes. Stack: Java, Spring Boot, JUnit, Kafka, Kubernetes, React.js, Node.js, MongoDB, Redis, BullMQ, FFmpeg. Repository: github.com/NagaSaiRam89/rivora-spring.

On Rivora, heavy media processing was holding up every request while it ran. He moved that work into the background so users get an answer immediately, which made responses 40 percent faster. Yes, he has used Kafka in production on this project, as the backbone carrying work between the Spring Boot core and the Node.js workers.

Rivora lost zero recordings across more than 100 sessions on unreliable connections, because audio saves in small pieces that retry on their own and stitch back together when the connection returns. This is a concrete example of designing for failure rather than assuming the happy path.

SnapStudy AI is a document processing app that took first place, working solo, at the Connect N Code Hackathon 2026, which was sponsored by Google Gemini. He went from idea to a deployed demo inside the competition window. Stack: React.js, TypeScript, Google Gemini API, Tesseract OCR, PDF.js. Repository: github.com/ramhere939/snapstudyai.

SnapStudy AI chains OCR into model calls to pull structured data out of handwritten notes and PDFs of 50 or more pages, then turns the extracted topics into a study plan. PDF.js reads the text layer where a PDF has one; Tesseract OCRs the pages and photos where it does not. Both input paths converge on plain text before Gemini sees anything.

The central design decision in SnapStudy AI is where the model stops. Gemini handles extraction, which genuinely needs judgement because no parser survives real handwriting. The scheduling logic stays a fixed algorithm rather than the model's judgement, so the same notes always produce the same study plan. Scheduling is arithmetic over topics, dates and weightings, and arithmetic belongs in code where it is deterministic, testable and cheap. Everything upstream of that boundary is probabilistic; everything downstream is not. There is a full case study of this on the portfolio at /case/snapstudy.
